beats.narration_text: Jambo. This is Liam, in for Bear, with chapter ten of INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about where a bar chart's axis starts. A bar measures its distance from the floor, not its value, so the floor sets the ratio you see. You'll watch two accuracies hold still while the floor slides. The trap: checking every number and never the floor.

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: Model B's bar is three times taller than Model A's. Is B three times better?
lines: A bar measures its distance from the axis floor, not its value, so the floor sets the ratio you see.
Watch 92.1% and 94.3% hold still while the floor slides: three times taller, then nearly equal.
The trap: checking every number on the chart and never checking where the axis starts.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? An AI will draw your chart and pick the axis floor for you, with no stake in whether the picture is honest. Miss the floor, and a two-point gain reaches a decision-maker as three times better. Check it, and you catch the argument before the chart makes it. And it unlocks the honest use: a raised floor when the range really is narrow.

beats.narration_text: Three terms you'll hear. The axis floor: the value where the vertical axis starts, the bottom edge every bar grows from. Accuracy: the share of test cases a model gets right, as a percentage. And a percentage point: the plain gap between two percentages. Ninety-four point three and ninety-two point one are two point two points apart.

the share of test cases a model gets right, as a percentage
the plain gap between two percentages: 94.3 and 92.1 are 2.2 points apart

learn.question: Every label on this chart is true. Is B three times better?
learn.action: Build the colleague's chart: axis 91–96, bars at 92.1 and 94.3.
learn.observation: B's bar is three times A's; the printed numbers are 2.2 points apart.
learn.inference: The picture and the numbers disagree, and neither is a typo.
learn.next_question: What exactly is the eye measuring?

beats.narration_text: A colleague slides a chart across the desk. Two models. Model A: ninety-two point one percent accurate. Model B: ninety-four point three. The axis runs from ninety-one to ninety-six. Every label on it is correct. And B's bar stands three times as tall as A's. So is B three times better? Nothing on this chart is false. Something on it is still lying to you.

shot.visual_intent: The colleague's chart builds: y-axis 91 at the floor, 96 at the top; bar A grows to 92.1%, bar B to 94.3%, each labelled; the right column reads 'looks ×3.0'; the caption 'Exercise 1 · constructed values' sits small at top right; the question 'three times better?' lands with a terracotta dot.

show.event: bar A grows to 92.1%, bar B to 94.3%

shot.motion_claim: The bars are the persistent objects; the question is unsolved.

learn.question: What is the eye measuring?
learn.action: Brace each bar from the floor to its top.
learn.inference: A bar's height is value minus floor.
learn.next_question: What happens if the floor moves and the values don't?

beats.narration_text: Measure what the eye measures. These bars don't start at zero; they start at ninety-one. So A's bar is ninety-two point one minus ninety-one: one point one. B's is ninety-four point three minus ninety-one: three point three. Three point three over one point one is exactly three. The eye isn't wrong about the bars. It's measuring from the floor.

shot.visual_intent: Floor 91 chart holds; a brace grows beside A's bar labelled '92.1 − 91 = 1.1', then beside B's '94.3 − 91 = 3.3'; the right column writes '3.3 ÷ 1.1 = 3'; caption: the eye measures from the floor.
shot.motion_claim: The first instance: the bar heights as measured from the floor, shown.

learn.question: What if only the floor moves?
learn.action: Slide the floor from 91 to 0 with the values fixed.
learn.observation: The height ratio falls from 3.0 to 1.02; the printed numbers never change.
learn.inference: The ratio the eye reads belongs to the floor, not to the data.
learn.next_question: But every number was true. Isn't that enough?

beats.narration_text: Now change one thing: the floor. Slide it down. Ninety. Eighty. Fifty. Zero. Watch the labels: ninety-two point one and ninety-four point three never move. The bars grow toward each other until, on a zero floor, B is one point oh two times A. Same data. The picture went from three times to almost nothing.

shot.visual_intent: The floor knob on the right rail slides 91 → 0 while the chart's floor label counts down and both bars grow toward equal height; the 'looks ×' readout counts 3.0 → 1.02; the two value labels ride their bar tops unchanged.
shot.motion_claim: The second instance: one parameter (the floor) varied continuously; the values are invariant.

learn.question: If every number is true, is the chart honest?
learn.observation: All three labels pass; the ×3 the eye reads was never printed.
learn.inference: A fact-check of the labels cannot catch a ratio the chart only implies.
learn.next_question: Where does the ×3 come from, mechanically?

beats.narration_text: Here's the defense you'll hear: every number on the chart is true, so the chart is honest. Check it. Ninety-two point one: true. Ninety-four point three: true. An axis from ninety-one to ninety-six: true. Every check passes, and the eye still reads three times. The numbers are true. The ratio the eye reads is not, and nobody printed that ratio.

shot.visual_intent: Back on the floor-91 chart; the right column lists three checks — '92.1% · true', '94.3% · true', 'axis 91 to 96 · true' — each with an ink check mark; then 'the eye reads ×3' with a terracotta X beside it; caption: true labels, false ratio.
shot.motion_claim: The natural defense walked to its limit: every printed fact checks out, the unprinted ratio does not.

learn.question: Where does the ×3 come from?
learn.action: Split each zero-floor bar at 91; discard below, stretch above.
learn.observation: Both bars lose the same 91; the slivers are 1.1 and 3.3.
learn.inference: Subtracting the same amount from both hits the smaller bar harder.
learn.next_question: So where must the floor sit for any ratio you want?

beats.narration_text: Here's the reframe. Go back to a zero floor and draw a line across both bars at ninety-one. Below the line, each bar holds exactly the same ninety-one. Above it, slivers: one point one and three point three. Now cut. The shared ninety-one drops away, and what's left is stretched to fill the frame. A truncated axis is a zoom on the slivers. The floor decides where the slivers begin.

shot.visual_intent: Zero-floor chart; a dashed ink line at 91 crosses both bars; the parts below turn ghost and each is labelled '91'; the slivers above stay ink with '1.1' and '3.3'; then the ghost parts sink away while the slivers stretch to fill the frame and become the floor-91 bars; 'looks ×3.0' returns.

show.event: ghost '91' below in both bars; slivers 1.1 and 3.3
the cut: ghost parts drop, slivers stretch
caption: a zoom on the slivers

shot.motion_claim: The representation: every bar = a shared part below the floor (thrown away) + a sliver above it (stretched).

learn.question: Which way, and how far, for ×2?
learn.action: Hold the picture with a twice-A guide.
learn.inference: A prediction turns the sweep into evidence.

beats.narration_text: Before it moves, commit. The floor sits at ninety-one, and B looks three times A. Where does the floor have to go for B to look exactly twice A? Up or down? And by how much: a point or two, or tens of points?

shot.visual_intent: The floor-91 chart holds; a dim dashed guide marks twice A's bar height, and B's top sits above it; the readout shows a target '×2 ?'; a dot on the rail knob; caption: commit before it moves.

learn.question: How much of the picture does the floor control?
learn.observation: The same two values read ×2, ×1.18, ×1.02 and ×23.
learn.inference: The visible ratio is a design choice; the data only fixes the labels.

beats.narration_text: Watch. Down to eighty-nine point nine: exactly twice. That's all it took, one point one. Eighty: one point one eight. Zero: one point oh two. Now up, toward A itself. At ninety-two, B looks twenty-three times A. The two numbers never moved. One setting the chart-maker picks did all of it.

shot.visual_intent: One continuous floor sweep through the persistent chart: 91 → 89.9 (looks ×2.0, the guide meets B's top) → 80 (×1.18) → 0 (×1.02) → up to 92 (×23, A's bar a sliver); the value labels 92.1% and 94.3% ride unchanged throughout; 'the numbers never moved' lands.
shot.motion_claim: The aha: one designer-chosen parameter spans ×1.02 to ×23 on the same data; narration short, the sweep gets the seconds.

learn.question: What is the rule?
learn.action: Write the height ratio in terms of B, A and the floor.
learn.observation: The floor appears in the numerator and the denominator.
learn.inference: Raising the floor always inflates the ratio in favour of the larger value.
learn.next_question: What does each symbol mean, exactly?

beats.narration_text: This deserves its name: a truncated axis, and here is its rule. The ratio your eye reads is B minus the floor, over A minus the floor. The floor sits in both, so it comes off both, and it hits the smaller bar harder. Floor at zero, you read the true ratio. Raise it, and the ratio grows without limit as the floor closes on A.

shot.visual_intent: The floor-91 chart holds at left; the right column assembles the rule term by term — looks = (B − floor) / (A − floor) — with a label under each piece (B's bar · A's bar · the same floor twice); 'truncated axis' lands bold; a terracotta dot beside the denominator on 'closes on A'.
shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as the name for what was watched.

learn.question: What does each symbol mean?
learn.action: Translate both sides; plug in the three floors.

beats.narration_text: Read the line. Left: the ratio the eye reads, B's bar over A's bar. Top: B minus the floor, which is B's bar. Bottom: A minus the floor, which is A's bar. The floor appears twice, the same number both times. That's the whole trick. Plug in. Floor ninety-one: three point three over one point one, three. Floor zero: ninety-four point three over ninety-two point one, one point oh two. Floor eighty-nine point nine: four point four over two point two, two. The numbers the sweep showed you.

shot.visual_intent: Split stage: the rule persists on the left; the right band writes the LHS sentence, the numerator and denominator glosses, 'the same floor twice'; then three worked values land under the rule: 3.3/1.1 = 3, 94.3/92.1 ≈ 1.02, 4.4/2.2 = 2.

show.event: worked values land one by one

shot.motion_claim: The equation tangent: formula, sentence, glossary, worked values.

learn.question: So — is B three times better?
learn.action: Read the hook chart with the floor in mind; print the gap; drop the floor.
learn.inference: The floor is an argument; state it or remove it.

beats.narration_text: Back to the colleague's chart. Floor at ninety-one, three times. Now you can read it: B is two point two percentage points higher, and the picture called it three times. When the question is how much better, drop the floor to zero, or print the gap. Truncation isn't banned. Stock prices live on raised floors, because zero means nothing there. The pixels look the same either way. The choice is the difference. Not taught here: side-by-side panels with different floors.

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK chart returns at floor 91 (looks ×3.0); a brace between the two bar tops reads '+2.2 points'; the floor slides to 0 and the bars settle nearly equal with '+2.2 points' riding; 'the choice is the difference' lands; boundary caption: not taught here: mismatched panels.
shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's bars resolve; the boundary names the transfer exercise.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A bar's height is its value minus the axis floor, so the floor is inside every bar. On a ninety-one floor, ninety-two point one and ninety-four point three look three to one; on a zero floor, one point oh two. The numbers never moved. The ratio the eye reads is B minus the floor over A minus the floor, and it grows without limit as the floor nears A. Truncation is honest when the range is narrow or zero means nothing. The pixels can't tell you which. The choice is the difference.

artifactLines: A bar's height is its value minus the axis floor. The floor is inside every bar.
Floor 91: 92.1% and 94.3% look 3 to 1. Floor 0: 1.02 to 1. The numbers never moved.
The eye reads (B − floor) / (A − floor), and it grows without limit as the floor nears A.
Truncation is honest when the range is narrow or zero means nothing. The choice is the difference.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: A dashboard shows three subgroup accuracy charts side by side. Group A's y-axis runs from 70 to 100 percent, Group B's from 85 to 100, Group C's from 60 to 100. A reviewer says the three groups look about the same. Before computing anything, predict: if each group's bar reaches the same fraction of its own panel, which group's accuracy is actually highest, and which lowest? Then use the rule that a bar's height is its value minus its axis floor to check your prediction, name the misleading choice, and describe the single change that would make the comparison valid. Two things to look for. Did it predict before it computed? If it jumped to numbers, send it back. And is its fix one shared axis for all three panels, not a note in the footer?
